title: Stories of the grammarians
summary: The famous reports (akhbār) the ṭabaqāt books tell of the grammarians: how naḥw began, how al-Khalīl found the metres, Sībawayh's defeat in Baghdad, al-Mubarrad's first circle, the raisin and the sour grape. Told as the sources tell them, as reports, not as certain history.

sections.heading: Reading the akhbār
paragraphs: The books of ṭabaqāt are not only lists of teachers and students. They are full of akhbār, short reports of what a grammarian said or did, each with its chain of tellers: a debate before a vizier, a mistake heard in the street, a sharp answer. The grammarians told them to each other for the same reasons people tell stories about their teachers anywhere: to show what the science is for, who was right, and how a scholar should behave.

Many are told in more than one version, and some were written down a century or two after the men they are about. Here they are told as the sources tell them, with the source named; where the versions differ, so do we. They are reports, not certain history.

sections.heading: Abū al-Aswad and the beginning of naḥw
paragraphs: Every ṭabaqāt begins with Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī in Basra. Al-Zubaydī gives several reasons why he began. In al-Mubarrad's report, Abū al-Aswad said that he had his first principles from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. In another, his daughter said mā ashaddu al-ḥarri, 'what is the hottest part of the heat?', when she meant mā ashadda al-ḥarra, 'how hot it is!', and he wrote the chapter of wonder. In a third, a man before the governor Ziyād said tuwuffiya abānā wa-taraka banūn, getting both endings wrong, and Ziyād, who had refused before, told Abū al-Aswad to write for the people what he had asked to write.

Ibn al-Anbārī's Nuzhat al-alibbāʾ, two centuries after al-Zubaydī, tells the fuller story later books repeat: ʿAlī gave Abū al-Aswad a sheet that began 'speech is all noun, verb and particle', and told him to follow that way (unḥu hādhā al-naḥw). Whatever its age, the story says what the grammarians believed: that their science began in the first generation of Islam, to protect the Qurʾān and the language from error.

sections.heading: Al-Khalīl and the beat of the hammers
paragraphs: Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad set out the metres of Arabic poetry in a system of feet and circles no one had made before him. Al-Zubaydī says simply that he drew out prosody as no one had. The later biographers add two stories: that he prayed at Mecca for a science no one had found before, and that the idea came to him as he walked through the market of the coppersmiths in Basra and heard the rhythm of their hammers. Both are told by later writers, and neither can be checked; but they fit the man al-Zubaydī describes, who refused a governor's money, kept only the fruit he had been sent, and answered in verse that wealth is in the soul.

sections.heading: Sībawayh: a mistake, a teacher and a defeat
paragraphs: Sībawayh came to Basra, a young Persian, to write down hadith. Al-Zubaydī tells that he was reading out a hadith in the circle of Ḥammād ibn Salama and corrected laysa Abā al-Dardāʾ to laysa Abū al-Dardāʾ; Ḥammād told him he had made a mistake, since laysa here means 'except'. 'I shall seek a knowledge in which you cannot fault me,' said Sībawayh, and went to al-Khalīl. Al-Khalīl, another report says, greeted him with words he used for no one else: 'Welcome to a visitor who never tires us.'

Years later he went to Baghdad, where al-Kisāʾī, the Kufan, taught the caliph's sons. Al-Zubaydī gives three versions of their meeting before the Barmakid vizier Yaḥyā ibn Khālid, the masʾala zunbūriyya. Al-Kisāʾī asked: 'I thought the scorpion stung harder than the hornet, and lo, it is he, or lo, it is her?' (fa-idhā huwa hiya, or fa-idhā huwa iyyāhā). Sībawayh allowed only the first; al-Kisāʾī both. Bedouin waiting at the door were asked and sided with al-Kisāʾī. Sībawayh was paid ten thousand dirhams and left; he went to Persia and, the reports say, died there of grief, young. His followers, al-Zubaydī adds, never doubted that he had been right, and said the Bedouin were men al-Kisāʾī knew.

In one version the story goes on in the words of al-Akhfash, Sībawayh's student. He went to Baghdad, prayed behind al-Kisāʾī, and put a hundred questions to him, faulting every answer. When al-Kisāʾī's students made to rise against him, al-Kisāʾī asked, 'Are you Abū al-Ḥasan Saʿīd ibn Masʿada?', embraced him, and asked him to teach his sons.

sections.heading: Al-Mubarrad's first circle
paragraphs: After the caliph al-Mutawakkil was murdered in 247/861, al-Mubarrad came to Baghdad poor and unknown. Al-Zubaydī tells that after the Friday prayer he began to explain grammar aloud, as if someone had asked him, until a circle formed. Thaʿlab, the master of the Kufans, sent two students to break it up. One of them, al-Zajjāj, asked a question; al-Mubarrad answered it, then showed what was wrong with his own answer, then set it right again, fourteen times over. Al-Zajjāj told his friends to go back without him: 'I speak of knowledge and reasoning, not of fame.' He stayed with al-Mubarrad, earning his living cutting glass a few days a month.

For nearly forty years the two masters taught in the same city, and their rivalry runs through every history of the grammarians. Al-Zubaydī reports one judgement of them: Thaʿlab was as sparing of words as al-Mubarrad and wider in learning, but he answered by hints, never plainly.

sections.heading: Al-Māzinī and the slave-girl's rajulan
paragraphs: The biographers tell of al-Māzinī, the Basran author of the first book on ṣarf, that he refused a hundred dinars to teach Sībawayh's book to a man of another faith, since it quotes the Qurʾān. Soon after, a slave-girl sang before the caliph al-Wāthiq a line that began 'O wronging one, your striking down a man (rajulan) who greeted you…'. Someone corrected her to rajulun; she held to rajulan and named al-Māzinī as her teacher. He was sent for, explained that rajulan is the object of the maṣdar muṣābakum, and went home with a thousand dinars: the hundred he had refused, as the story says, ten times over.

sections.heading: The raisin and the sour grape
paragraphs: Ibn Jinnī was teaching grammar in the mosque of Mosul when Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī came by. As Yāqūt tells it, al-Fārisī heard him explain how the wāw becomes alif in qāla and qāma, put an objection to him that he could not answer, and said: 'You have turned to raisin while still a sour grape' (tazabbabta wa-anta ḥiṣrim). Ibn Jinnī asked who the stranger was, left his circle, and followed him for forty years. Ibn Khallikān tells it otherwise: Ibn Jinnī had studied with al-Fārisī before and set up on his own too soon. The question of qāla stayed with him; his books come back to it again and again.

sections.heading: Two later stories
paragraphs: Ibn Mālik opens his Alfiyya by saying that it surpasses the Alfiyya of Ibn Muʿṭī, and then grants Ibn Muʿṭī the merit of coming first. The commentators tell that after the first verse he could not go on until Ibn Muʿṭī appeared to him in a dream and reproached him, and that he then wrote the verse of acknowledgement. It is told as a lesson in courtesy to one's predecessors.

In Mamluk Cairo, the biographers tell, Khālid al-Azharī was a lamp-lighter in al-Azhar. A wick fell from his hand onto a student's notes; the student called him ignorant, and he began to study, by these reports at thirty-six. He became the author of al-Taṣrīḥ and of the commentary on al-Ājurrūmiyya that the madrasas still read.
